chapter: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
title: Playing to dancers' favorite tunes and clubs that interfere
summary: Survival means playing familiar standards like Peg O' My Heart that fill the floor. Some clubs respect his judgment; Denver operators try to run the band.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Uh-huh. Do you -- I'm sure that as a leader at the present time, that you're conscious pretty much of the time when you're playing a job, that you're conscious of what the business, how it's doing and how the club owner feels and that you're making every effort to satisfy your listeners, as well as the club owner. Do you feel that you're more conscious of this now then you were, say, in the '20's or '30's when you had your bands then?

Well, yes, I am because, unfortunately, it's a matter of survival, you know. However, we don't go overboard to do it. What we try to do, and I've talked to my fellows about this, my boys in the band, that is. We usually have quite a few arrangements in the book that -- I won't say the style of the band changes, but we found out one thing. It seems like the people here that go out and support these clubs, we found out -- the real dancers, even in the settled bunch -- they seem to dance by the names of tunes. You know, if they know a tune, and you play a little melody and things like that, man, they used to flow right away. And you can turn right around there and play something else that is a swinger, or either

a great tune, one of those things. If they don't know it, they sit this one out, you know, and they'll applaud after you finish. But as soon as you go into one of the old standards, something that -- like Peg O' My Heart, things that never die, and you play that melody, man, before you get to the first eight bars, the floor's half filled. And it's a great thing. So we found out if this is the type of thing they like, and we hit them with that, we stick with it because we've got a book full of those things.

And then a lot of times we might start out another way, and we found out it isn't getting through to the people. We change the tunes. We try some other things, you know. And whenever we get something where we hit them with it, we stay there, and so this naturally makes the boss happy.

And they notice all of these things. But here recently I've been playing some nice clubs where they don't bother us at all. They hired us because they respected my judgment on how to reach the public, and we've been successful in it, and they don't interrupt us, you know. That is the -- one of the reasons why I like to play the surrounding towns, because they do give you more liberties as a band-leader, because they respect your judgment in judging the audience, while here in Denver the night club operators, they

try to run your band, some of them, and they try to -- like they try to run the bartenders and have certain things, which is all right with me, as far as if they knew what they were doing. But I've found out through experience that it just isn't there, and if you follow the pattern that they want, you're out. This is what it winds up -- they blame you. They don't stop to think that they're the cause of these things, you know. So I just try to avoid these guys, you know.
